reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of the bifunctional enzyme glutamate formiminotransferase-cyclodeaminase (FTCD), which transfers a formimino group from formiminoglutamate to tetrahydrofolate in the histidine degradation and folate pathways
The characteristic biochemical finding is increased urinary excretion of formiminoglutamate (FIGLU), classically enhanced after an oral histidine load
Clinical significance is uncertain and probably mild in many cases; reported phenotypes range from apparently benign to variable developmental delay and haematological changes
A severe and a mild form have been described, and the disorder is considered one of the more common but least clinically clear-cut inborn errors of folate metabolism
Serum folate may be normal or high because the folate-dependent step is blocked downstream, distinguishing it from dietary folate deficiency
There is no firmly established specific therapy; folate/folinic acid supplementation has been used empirically
British spelling and paediatric context apply where relevant
reference.pathophysiology: Histidine is degraded via urocanate and formiminoglutamate (FIGLU), and the final step requires glutamate formiminotransferase to transfer FIGLU's formimino group onto tetrahydrofolate, linking histidine catabolism to one-carbon folate metabolism. Deficiency of the FTCD enzyme blocks this transfer, so FIGLU accumulates and is excreted, particularly after a histidine load, while one-carbon units that would have entered the folate pool are not efficiently captured. Because the block is downstream of folate, circulating folate is often not low, and the overall clinical impact appears variable and frequently mild, which is why the disorder's pathogenicity remains debated.
additionalDifferentials: Dietary or malabsorptive folate deficiency (also raises FIGLU excretion)
Vitamin B12 deficiency affecting folate-dependent metabolism
Other inborn errors of folate metabolism (e.g. MTHFR deficiency)
Benign biochemical findings on metabolic screening
Coincidental developmental disorder of separate cause
Liver disease altering histidine and folate handling
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic/amino acid analysis for formiminoglutamate, ideally after a histidine load
Serum and red-cell folate and vitamin B12 levels
Full blood count and film for megaloblastic or other changes
Molecular analysis of the FTCD gene
Assessment of dietary folate intake to exclude nutritional cause
redFlags: Significant developmental delay prompting evaluation for other causes
Haematological abnormality such as megaloblastic change requiring investigation
Assuming pathogenicity and over-treating what may be a benign finding
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally thought to be good, with many individuals mildly affected or asymptomatic, though the true clinical significance of the biochemical defect remains uncertain. Management is supportive and empirical.
pitfalls: Confusing raised FIGLU excretion from nutritional folate deficiency with the inherited enzyme defect
Over-attributing developmental problems to an uncertain biochemical finding
Assuming low folate when serum folate is often normal or high
Failing to consider vitamin B12 deficiency in the interpretation
references: Scriver's OMMBID: disorders of folate metabolism and FTCD deficiency
Nyhan, Atlas of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: Offer empirical folate or folinic acid supplementation, as no specific proven therapy exists and the enzymatic block lies downstream of the folate pool
Ensure an adequate dietary folate intake and exclude a coexisting nutritional deficiency
Monitor the full blood count and film for megaloblastic or other haematological changes
Provide developmental assessment and early-intervention therapies where developmental delay is present
Give genetic counselling and offer family testing for this autosomal recessive FTCD disorder
Follow up through a metabolic medicine service, avoiding overtreatment given the uncertain clinical significance of the biochemical defect
